tagline.text: A remote island in western Mindoro with Onoda's jungle trail and a Spanish-era lighthouse

location.label: Location
location.text: Northwest of Mindoro Island; two municipalities, Lubang and Looc, in Occidental Mindoro

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱3,000~8,000 (per person, boat, lodging, meals and local transport)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), then overland and by boat

children.text: Lubang Island is the largest island of the Lubang group northwest of mainland Mindoro, about 117 km southwest of Manila. It keeps the jungle trail where Lieutenant Onoda hid until 1974, a Spanish-era lighthouse and white-sand beaches, which suits travelers looking for a quiet island trip.
Lubang Island is the largest of the seven islands of the Lubang group in Occidental Mindoro. According to Wikipedia, it lies northwest of the northern tip of mainland Mindoro, about
40 km
west of Calatagan in Batangas and about
117 km
southwest of Manila. Sources disagree on its area: many give about 125 square kilometers, while others say 250 square kilometers. The highest point is Mount Ambonong at about

. The 2020 population was about 20,000 (20,436), and the island is divided into two municipalities: Lubang in the northwestern half and Looc in the rest. Lubang has the main port, Tilik Port, where most residents and travelers pass through, and Looc has Agkawayan Port, a second gateway. Looc also administers the rest of the island and nearby islands such as Ambil and Golo.

The main reason travelers know this island is the story of Lieutenant Hiroo Onoda, a Japanese military intelligence officer. He kept hiding and fighting in the forests of Lubang even after World War II ended and surrendered only in March 1974, 29 years after the war. The story inspired the 2016 film Onoda's War, the 2021 film Onoda: 10,000 Nights in the Jungle and Werner Herzog's novel The Twilight World. The island has the Onoda Trail, which follows the paths he used. His story is more than a war tale; it shows how deep and remote the island's forests are. The fact that he could avoid people for so many years suggests how rugged the paths and how dense the forest were. If you listen to a guide's account of those days as you walk, the trail takes on a different meaning.

The island also holds traces of the Spanish era. At the entrance to Tilik Port stands the San Vicente Bastion, built by the Spanish, and on Cabra Island stands a lighthouse more than 100 years old, described as one of the few Spanish-era lighthouses still standing. Most of the coast is white sand, and residents live by fishing and by growing rice, garlic, peanuts and vegetables. Because it sits at the western end of the Verde Island Passage, its waters are said to be rich in marine life, and some animals, such as the Lubang forest mouse, live only on this island. Historical accounts say the group was settled early by the ancestors of the Tagalog people and was an early trading point with Chinese merchants. Tourism is slowly growing, but there are still no large resorts, so a quiet atmosphere remains.

This guide is for travelers who can spare a day or two beyond Manila to visit a quiet island away from crowded tourist spots. Know a few things first. The island has almost no scheduled public transport, boats are affected by weather and waves, and some of the lodging and boat information used here dates from 2013–2014. Always reconfirm fares and schedules locally before you leave. With that in mind, Lubang offers a taste of the Philippines' lesser-known island travel.
The trail runs from Barangay Vigo in Lubang to the neighboring town of Looc, and walking all of it is said to take three days. There is also a loop of about
8 km

that takes half a day. Many sections have no signs, so walking with a local guide is safer. The forest changes from section to section and gives a chance to see birds and endemic animals, so bring binoculars. Before you walk, agree with your guide where you will start and finish and how transport will connect.

This Spanish-era lighthouse, more than 100 years old, is one of the places island visitors go most often. Cabra Island is a small island belonging to Lubang, so you need to hire a boat, and on days with high waves you may not be able to go. The sea views on the way and the shallow waters nearby are good, so many people add snorkeling. When you hire a boat, agree on life jackets and the return time before leaving.

Tagbac and Binacas in Lubang and Bonbon in Looc are the best known. The sand is fine and there are few people, so they are good for snorkeling and free diving. Some beaches are known as sea turtle nesting sites.
This Spanish-era fort guarded the entrance to Tilik Port, the main port. You meet the island's history as soon as you step off the boat, so it is a nice light stop on the day you arrive.
Inland there is Hulagaang Falls, and treks lead to the Gozar Air Station site, Mount Benogongon and Mount Gonting. The paths are unclear, so you need a guide.
Some of the beach resorts run a dive center, and scuba diving is said to be bookable there. Underwater shipwrecks are also mentioned, but confirm their location and safety with a local operator.

The island has endemic species such as the Lubang forest mouse, the Lubang scaly-toed gecko and the Lubang slender skink, and Philippine cobras and many birds are said to live there. On forest paths, watch for snakes and follow your guide's instructions.

items.subtitle: A day at the port and the beach

children.text: Travel overland from Manila to Calatagan or Nasugbu and take the boat to Lubang. Departures change with the weather, so check with the boat owner the day before.
Arrive at Tilik Port, drop your bags at your lodging and look around the San Vicente Bastion.
Swim and snorkel at Tagbac Beach and watch the sunset.
On the morning of the second day, walk the loop of the Onoda Trail for half a day with a guide.
After lunch, return to Tilik Port and take the boat back.
Even if a boat schedule is set, trips can be canceled because of waves, so an itinerary with a spare day is safer.
Arrive at Tilik Port, see the San Vicente Bastion and the town, and rest at your lodging
Hike the Onoda Trail with a guide, trekking toward the Gozar Air Station site
Hire a boat to the Cabra Island lighthouse and snorkel in nearby waters
See the southern beaches such as Bonbon Beach in Looc and depart from the port
Getting around the island by tricycle, van or hired boat is the realistic choice. Book guides and transport in advance through the tourism office or your lodging.

items.title: From Manila to Calatagan or Nasugbu

children.text: From Taft Avenue in Manila, a bus or van is said to take about
3 hours
to Calatagan and about
2 hours
to Nasugbu. It varies with traffic.
From Calatagan or Nasugbu there are boats to Tilik Port in Lubang or to Agkawayan Port in Looc. Wikivoyage lists boats from Nasugbu to Tilik Port.
Which port has a boat running changes over time, so check with the boat owner or the tourism office before you leave.

A 2013 source says wooden pump boats (such as MB God's Grace 2) ran from Calatagan to Tilik Port on set days, with a one-way fare of about ₱500. Reports say the crossing takes 3 to 4 hours depending on sea conditions.

The same source also lists an Atienza Shipping Lines boat between Manila and Tilik (leaving Manila Monday at noon and Tilik Tuesday at 9:00 AM). This information is old, so be sure to check whether it still runs and the current fare.
Many reports say boats do not leave on schedule. Book early in the summer peak season and on holidays.
At Tilik Port you can hire tricycles, vans and boats. The island is said to have almost no scheduled public transport.
Lubang Airport (LBX) exists, but it has no scheduled flights and is used only by charter flights.
This is an island you reach by boat, so weather matters most. In the dry season, December–May, the sea is relatively calm, which makes boat trips, beaches and treks easier.

In the rainy and typhoon season, June–November, waves are high and boats may be canceled, and forest paths are slippery. If you go then, keep your schedule loose and leave a spare day before you return.

The 2013 source lists Lubang Bay Hotel near Tilik Port and resorts on Tagbac Beach (such as Don Juan Villa Beach Resort). Some run a dive center, and the guesthouse at Binacas Beach is said to be hard to reach. There are also homestays, which the tourism office can arrange. Contact numbers and rates are out of date, so check the latest information.

There is not much information on restaurants. Because this is an island with seafood and local produce (rice, garlic, peanuts), meals are often taken at your lodging, and it is safer to bring snacks and water in advance.
Bring plenty of cash. Reports say there is no ATM and that no one accepts cards or traveler's checks.
Mobile signal is weak. Reports say Globe has no signal in particular, so check your carrier beforehand.
Electricity runs 24 hours but power cuts are said to be frequent. Bring a power bank.
Many sections of the Onoda Trail have no signs. Go with a trained local guide.
Boats leave according to weather and tides. Do not schedule anything important on your return day.
Be careful of strong currents after storms when swimming, and do not go to isolated beaches alone at night. Reports mention little lighting and wild dogs.
Transport on the island is described as tricycles, vans and boats. Ask your lodging whether vehicles can be rented.
On the way from Manila, stay a night in Nasugbu or Calatagan and take an early boat for a less rushed trip.
The tourism office is said to connect travelers with trained guides for the Onoda Trail. Contact them in advance to set the date and route.
This is a remote island with almost no scheduled public transport and few banks. Leave a spare day on your return in case boats are canceled.
Some boat and lodging prices in this guide come from 2013–2014. Recheck all fares and schedules before you leave.
We could not confirm the island's medical facilities. Bring a first-aid kit and travel insurance.
Philippine cobras are said to live in the forest. Do not enter the forest without a guide.
Do not touch eggs or hatchlings on beaches where sea turtles nest.
A port town from which boats to Lubang leave, about
3 hours
from Manila by road. It is also good for a night's stay before departure.
An island off Batangas that is part of the same Verde Island Passage as the Lubang group, known for rich marine life.
A well-known beach resort in northern Mindoro, which some travelers combine with Lubang.
A large port city on the route from Manila to Mindoro, and a possible starting point for a Lubang trip.
